title: A polynomial time algebraic solution to exact marginal inference in Markov Random Field models
abstract: This paper develops on algebraic grounds a polynomial time exact linear solution to the hard combinatorial problem of marginal inference in Markov random field (MRF) models under general assumptions. To prove our claim, we first implicitly remodel a MRF joint distribution as the unique solution of some linear identity assuming its clique potential functions (equivalently, its individual conditional distributions) to be specified. Then, by assuming an arbitrary point subset, we relax accordingly such a (global) linear identity for deriving a second linear identity, solely, acting on a polynomial time number of entries (e.g.; local marginals or Fourier frequencies) of a solution. Then, we show, only using linear algebraic techniques, that such an identity enables to capture all the entries necessary for the exact reconstruction of an MRF marginal distribution, thus, allowing to solve for the latter, exactly and in polynomial time, using a standard linear solver. Last, but not least, this paper probably solves, once and for all, the P = NP conjecture.

sections.heading: Introduction
sections.text: Markov random fields (MRFs) [3, 14, 15, 25, 36, 56, 57] are a powerful modern probabilistic modeling tool both in theoretical and applied sciences [5, 32, 37, 60]. Conceptually, MRFs are multivariate random variables which are a natural generalization of Markov chains to multiple dimensions (e.g.; space). Thus, the dependency structure of a MRF is represented by an undirected graph instead of a directed 1𝐷chain, and the causality property which is intrinsic of Markov chains is substituted in a MRF with the local Markov property. The latter implies the concept of neighborhood, and suggests that each random variable is conditionally independent of all the other random variables which are not in its neighborhood given only the ones which are in its neighborhood. An intermediary class of graphical models is the Bayesian network class [32, 46]. Like the MRFs, Bayesian networks are also multidimensional, and graph-representable (but, rather by a directed acyclic graph), except that, like Markov chains, they enjoy the causality property [45]. The latter implies the notion of parenthood, and suggests that each random variable is conditionally independent of its non-descendants given its immediate parents. sections.text: 0:2 • Ikhlef Bechar the causality assumption has dramatic consequences on the way Bayesian networks are learned, simulated, and used for inference [4, 32, 45, 47]. Naturally, all the developed results in this paper regarding the general MRF framework apply effortlessly to the general Bayesian framework too. Historically, MRFs have been originated independently in statistical physics and in probability theory. In statistical physics [19] where they have been mostly known as Gibbsian fields, they had been originally developed for describing thermodynamic (macroscopic) equilibrium states of large systems of interacting tiny particles (e.g.; electrons, atoms, molecules, etc) [16, 28, 31, 49]. Their surge in probability theory and computer science has been, however, more progressive [18, 58]. Originally, Markov developed in the early 1950s the notion of conditional independence, and suggested how some complex probabilistic models can sometimes be explained in terms of a chain of simple dependencies using the chain rule of probability theory, and the notion of conditional independence [40]. However, it was not until the late 1960s, with the surge of computer science, that the notion of MRF started to take shape. Hence, in 1968, Dobrushin introduced the concepts of infinite Gibbsian state and of a Markov random field [14, 15]. In 1970, Spitzer suggested that the random field of interacting Markovian processes on a cubic lattice, assuming binary interactions, is Gibbsian [56]. A year later, Hammersley and Clifford proved Gibbs-Markov equivalence (or, the MRF consistency theorem) under the positivity assumption about a distribution suggesting that any positive Markovian distribution is Gibbsian, and reciprocally [25]. However, Hammersley and Clifford never published their theorem thinking that the positivity assumption is too restrictive from a physical standpoint. But later in 1974, Besag revamped the proof of their theorem, moreover, proved that the positivity assumption about a joint distribution is not simply sufficient, but, it is also necessary. He also suggested that a MRF distribution is uniquely determined by its individual conditional distributions [3]. In a way, this has been a noticeable step forward as it makes it possible to completely and uniquely specify any joint MRF distribution simply by means of local (clique) interactions between random variables. In 1984, Geman and Geman popularized MRFs in computer science with their influential paper [18]. Since then, MRFs have reached out to disciplines as diverse as statistics [4, 29, 45, 48], information theory [35, 59, 65], artificial intelligence [9, 12, 46, 47], computer vision and machine learning [1, 5, 39, 60, 63], biostatistics [53, 61], social networks [50], and so forth. However, a fundamental problem which has tapped, so far, the minds of many researchers concerns inference computation in MRF models, whether it is Maximum-A-Posteriori (MAP) inference where the goal is computation of the most likely assignment, marginal inference where the goal is computation of MRF marginal distributions over arbitrary small subsets of random variables, evaluation of the normalizing constant of a MRF distribution (also referred, using statistical physics terminology, as the partition function), hence, pointwise evaluation of a MRF distribution too, and so forth. It is then well-known that the problem of evaluation of the partition function is polynomial time reducible to the marginal inference problem in a MRF model. Hence, a polynomial-time procedure to solve the former can be recycled for solving the latter in polynomial-time. The converse of the latter statement also turns out to be true [8]. Nonetheless, it is a well established fact that either of the aforementioned inference problems is, in general, a hard combinatorial problem [7, 9–13, 22, 30, 41, 51, 54]. More precisely, MAP inference in a general MRF model is NP hard since, for instance, the maximum independent set problem in an indirected graph (i.e.; the largest set of vertices in an indirected graph, such that, there exists no edge connecting any couple of its vertices) which is NP-hard [20, 30] can be reduced in polynomial time to a MAP inference problem in a proper MRF model with regard to the same undirected graph. Marginal inference in general MRF models is #-hard (Sharp-hard) since, for instance, the independent set counting problem in an indirected graph which is #-hard can be reduced in polynomial time to a marginal inference problem in a MRF model. One notes that hardness reductions to CPS (Constraint Satisfaction Problem) can be equally obtained [8]. The bottom line is that, unless P = NP, there exists literally no polynomial time algorithm which can solve either exactly, or at least, approximately a general instance of a marginal, or a MAP inference in a general MRF model. Nevertheless, there exists MRF instances (e.g.; MRFs Proc. ACM Meas. Anal. Comput. Syst., Vol. 0, No. 0, Article 0. Publication date: 2026. This explains why it is frequently stated in the literature that marginal inference is a harder problem than MAP inference in general MRF models. To cut a long story short, inference computation in a general MRF model has only been dealt heuristically so far. Since this paper is primarily concerned with the problem of marginal inference in MRF models, we refer the reader who is interested in MAP inference to the literature dealing with the topic. Basically, heuristical marginal inference approaches can be divided into two main categories, namely, stochastic sampling (MCMC) based [17, 23, 26, 63], and variational inference [29, 60, 65] algorithms. The latter category of approaches has, since recently, gained considerable interest among the research community mainly due to availability of fast mathematical programming solvers [2, 38, 43]. Their general principle is to replace a MRF model instance (in which inference computation is seemingly hard) with a surrogate model which is closest to it in some sense among a parametric family of models in which exact inference computation is easy (e.g.; a MRF model with regard to a tree), then perform inference directly with regard to the latter as a way to circumvent the situation. This is then achieved by optimizing an objective with respect to the parameters of a surrogate distribution, typically, a Bethe objective basically consisting of a Kullback-Leibler divergence term plus a proper penalty term. Furthermore, when optimization of the objective is performed using the gradient descent algorithm, solution updates are made in a way which is reminiscent of transmission of messages between nodes, hence also the name of message passing algorithms, or Loopy Belief Propagation (LBP) (said otherwise, Belief Propagation (BP) on graphs containing cycles) [47, 64, 65]. Variants of the latter include the tree-reweighted belief propagation (TRBP) algorithm [59], the convergent TRBP [33], convergent message-passing based on geometric programming [21], the dual decomposition algorithm [34, 55], to name a few. Although, except in a few particular cases (e.g.; tree-structured graphical models [46], factor graphs [35], and so forth), there is generally no guarantee for a good solution, or even of convergence [42, 62], it has been reported on multiple occasions that variational inference techniques can sometimes perform well empirically for applications ranging from information theory, to artificial intelligence, signal processing, to name a few [1, 21, 33, 34, 42, 59, 63]. In this paper, we attempt to take a step forward with regard to the existing literature, and we propose to solve the marginal inference problem in MRF models, exactly and in polynomial time, under rather general assumptions. More precisely, in order to work around the unwieldy combinatorics arising from the summation of a Gibbsian model over exponentially many assignments, as a first step, we reformulate a MRF marginal inference problem on purely linear algebraic grounds, more specifically, as the one consisting in computing the marginal over a given point subset of a function (i.e.; a joint MRF distribution) encoded, implicitly, as the unique solution of some linear identity. As a second step, we relax accordingly such a seemingly hard linear identity to an easy analog which, in contrast, admits an infinity of solutions, but which all share a common marginal over such an assumed point subset coinciding with the sought MRF marginal distribution. We then want to underline that this paper is self-contained, moreover, its content is accessible to a wide audience, in that: a) no background on marginal inference is, actually, required for catching up with the content of this paper; b) all our findings throughout are proved in detail, moreover, no external results are recycled throughout (except obviously well-known algebraic results); c) last, but, not least, all our proofs in this paper use basic notions of linear algebra and mathematical programming. The remainder of this paper is organized as follows. Section 2 states the MRF marginal inference problem in general terms. Section 4 fixes some of the definitions and notations of the paper. Section 3 succinctly and simply presents the main result in this paper. Sections 5 and 6 develop the polynomial time algebraic reformulation of a general MRF marginal inference problem. Section 7 discusses complexity and algorithmic resolution of MRF marginal inference computation. A discussion concludes this paper. Proc. ACM Meas. Anal. Comput. Syst., Vol. 0, No. 0, Article 0.
